tulu-3-pushing-frontiers-in-open-languag.oneSentence: Tülu 3 is the fully-open post-training playbook — curate → SFT → DPO → RLVR — that takes Llama 3.1 base models to state-of-the-art among open-weight models and documents every dataset, hyperparameter, and negative result.
tulu-3-pushing-frontiers-in-open-languag.summary: Tülu 3 is the reference recipe for the post-training half of this curriculum: it walks a pretrained base model through supervised finetuning, preference tuning with length-normalized DPO, and a new stage the authors call Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), releasing the data, code, evals, and intermediate checkpoints for each. RLVR is the piece that maps directly onto the lab's own Phase 13 work — the policy earns a fixed reward only when a deterministic verifier confirms its answer is correct (exact-match on GSM8K/MATH, constraint checkers for instruction following), and that binary signal is optimized with PPO under a KL penalty to a frozen reference. What makes the paper valuable as a teaching text is its honesty: it reports the SFT loss-aggregation bug it found and fixed, why it picked DPO over PPO for the preference stage, why disabling dropout matters for PPO's clip to behave, how over-optimization shows up as KL drift, and which ideas (online DPO, rejection sampling, mixing RM scores into RLVR) did not pay off.
coreIdeas: A modern open post-training pipeline is four sequential stages on top of a pretrained base — data curation, SFT, preference tuning (DPO), and RL on verifiable rewards — each building on the previous checkpoint.

RLVR replaces the learned reward model of classic RLHF with a deterministic verifier: reward = α if the completion is provably correct, else 0, optimized with PPO and a KL penalty to a reference policy.
Reproducibility is a first-class deliverable: releasing data, decontamination tooling, code, evals, and the negative results is what actually closes the gap between open and closed post-training.

Implementation details dominate outcomes — sum-vs-mean loss aggregation in SFT, length normalization in DPO, disabling dropout and penalizing non-EOS completions in PPO — small mechanics that quietly decide whether training works.
tulu-3-pushing-frontiers-in-open-languag.whyItMatters: Tülu 3 is the open playbook for the post-training half of this curriculum. Its SFT → DPO → RLVR arc is exactly the learner's Phase 9 → Phase 13 path, and its RLVR stage is precisely what the Phase 13 exercises implement: a verifiable_reward function, GRPO/PPO-style advantages, and a PPO clip around a KL-anchored reference. It gives a concrete, reproduced target — real numbers, real hyperparameters, and documented failure modes — for work the learner is otherwise building blind.
tulu-3-pushing-frontiers-in-open-languag.phaseConnection: Read it in Phase 9 (SFT) to anchor the supervised-finetuning stage — data mixing, sum-loss aggregation, batch size 128, 2 epochs — and again in Phase 13 (RL on verifiable tasks), where RLVR's objective (v(x,y)=α-if-correct-else-0 wrapped in PPO with a KL penalty) is the reference implementation for your verifiable_reward + advantage + PPO-clip exercises. Use its overoptimization finding (lower β → more KL drift → higher targeted score but lower average) as the health check when your own RLVR runs start gaming the verifier.
suggestedReadingFocus: The RLVR objective and verifier (Section 6, Eqs. 7-8) — the exact mechanism your Phase 13 code reimplements
The PPO stability details for RLVR — disable dropout, -10 non-EOS penalty, advantage whitening, value-init from a general RM
Length-normalized DPO (Section 5, Eq. 6) and the reasoning for choosing it over PPO in the preference stage
The SFT sum-loss vs. mean-loss fix (Section 4.3.2) as a concrete throw-an-error-not-a-fallback bug
The 'Insights from the Unfruitful' discussion (Section 8.2) — what did not improve performance and why

2-olmo-2-furious.oneSentence: OLMo 2 is a fully open family of dense 7B/13B/32B models — weights, all data, code, logs, and thousands of checkpoints — that reaches the performance-vs-FLOPs Pareto frontier by combining a stability-hardened pretraining recipe with a two-stage curriculum: a long web-data pretrain followed by a short mid-training anneal on the curated Dolmino Mix that infuses knowledge and patches math.
2-olmo-2-furious.summary: The OLMo Team release the most reproducible frontier-class training recipe in existence: not just weights but the entire pretraining and mid-training data, training and eval code, logs, and thousands of intermediate checkpoints. The report is built around two lessons the learner reproduces at single-GPU scale. First, pretraining stability — OLMo-0424 spiked in loss and gradient norm (worse at larger scale) until it diverged, so OLMo 2 applies a bundle of fixes measured by a 'spike score' (percent of values seven std from a rolling mean): a repeated-n-gram data filter, N(0, 0.02) initialization of all parameters, RMSNorm on the outputs of the attention and MLP blocks (reordered/post-norm), QK-norm, z-loss, no weight decay on embeddings, and AdamW epsilon lowered to 1e-8. Second, the mid-training recipe — after the web-heavy pretrain (>=90% of FLOPs), training restarts on the curated Dolmino Mix while the learning rate is linearly decayed to zero (5-10% of FLOPs). Data sources are vetted cheaply via 'microannealing' (mix a candidate ~50/50 with web, anneal small, read the benchmark delta), and several anneal runs on different data orders are averaged into a 'checkpoint soup.' Mid-training alone lifts the 7B average by 10.6 points — GSM8K 24.1 -> 67.5 — enough that the annealed 7B beats the pretrained 13B. A key annealing finding: linearly decaying any peak LR to zero makes final loss nearly invariant to the peak, and the crossover between learning rates sits well past 200B tokens, so short sweeps mislead.
coreIdeas: Two-stage curriculum: a long web-data pretrain (>=90% of FLOPs, cosine decay to ~10% of peak) then a short mid-training anneal (5-10%) on curated data with the LR linearly driven to zero — this staged shape IS the annealing story of phase 8.

Pretraining stability is a bundle, not a single fix: init N(0, 0.02), RMSNorm, reordered/post-norm, QK-norm, z-loss, no weight decay on embeddings, and AdamW eps=1e-8 — each targets a specific loss/gradient spike or slow-growth failure, tracked by an objective spike score.

Linear LR anneal to zero makes final loss nearly invariant to the peak learning rate, and higher LRs are overtaken by lower ones only well past 200B tokens — short hyperparameter experiments draw the wrong conclusion.

Data sources for mid-training can be assessed independently and cheaply via microannealing (~50/50 mix with web, small anneal run); domain data helps even in small proportions, light duplication helps, and rewriting code-form math into natural language dramatically lifts GSM8K.
Checkpoint souping — naively averaging models annealed on different data orders — reliably equals or beats the best single run, a free quality gain that scales down.
2-olmo-2-furious.whyItMatters: OLMo 2 is the most curriculum-aligned model family that exists: fully open data, code, checkpoints, and training logs mean the learner can compare their own runs against the real thing at every step. It documents, with ablations, exactly the two things phase 8 is about — the pretraining-stability interventions that keep a run from diverging, and the two-stage base-pretrain-then-mid-training-anneal curriculum that turns a mediocre base model into a competitive one. The 10.6-point jump from a short anneal, and the finding that final loss is nearly LR-invariant under linear decay, are the concrete payoffs that justify running the annealing stage at all.
2-olmo-2-furious.phaseConnection: Phase 8 (continued pretraining) reading. The learner runs a single-GPU version of exactly this recipe shape: pretrain a small model, then mid-train (anneal) it on a curated, up-sampled mixture with the LR linearly decayed to zero. Use OLMo 2 as the reference recipe — reproduce the stability checklist (Section 3), the linear anneal and its LR-plateau finding (Section 4.1), microannealing to vet a data source cheaply (Section 4.4.2), and checkpoint souping (Section 4.5) — and use the fully open logs and checkpoints to sanity-check the learner's own annealing curve.
suggestedReadingFocus: The two-stage recipe (Section 2.3 and Section 4): which stage builds which capability, the FLOP split, cosine-to-10% vs linear-to-zero schedules.
The stability bundle and spike score (Section 3): treat init, RMSNorm, reordered/post-norm, QK-norm, z-loss, no-WD-on-embeddings, and AdamW eps=1e-8 as a checklist tied to specific failure modes.
Learning-rate annealing (Section 4.1): linear decay to zero, near-invariance to peak LR, and the >200B-token crossover that warns against short sweeps.
Microannealing (Section 4.4.2) and checkpoint souping (Section 4.5): the cheap per-source evaluation primitive and the merge trick, both reproducible at small scale.

smollm2-when-smol-goes-big-data-centric-.oneSentence: SmolLM2 is data-centric small-model training done right: a 1.7B model deliberately over-trained on ~11T tokens via a four-stage data mixture that is manually rebalanced between stages, reserving newly-built high-quality math and code data for a final annealing phase.
smollm2-when-smol-goes-big-data-centric-.summary: SmolLM2 is the reference case study for the two things this lab cares about most: how you curate data (Phase 1) and how you keep improving a model after the bulk of pretraining (Phase 8). It trains a stock 1.7B Llama2-architecture model on roughly 11 trillion tokens — deliberate over-training at exactly the scale class Microlab works in — and shows that the wins come from data, not architecture. Rather than fixing one mixture for the whole run, the authors use a Warmup-Stable-Decay schedule and manually rebalance the dataset mixture across four stages in response to live benchmark signals: web text forms the backbone, medium-sized code and math datasets are introduced mid-training to avoid dilution, and the highest-quality math and code are withheld and upsampled during the final learning-rate decay. That staged mixing with an upsampled decay phase IS the annealing/midtraining concept Phase 8 teaches, made fully concrete. When existing datasets underperformed, they built new ones (FineMath, Stack-Edu, SmolTalk) using the same classifier-based educational-filtering pattern that anchors Phase 1 data quality.
coreIdeas: At small scale, data curation dominates architecture — limited capacity must be spent on core knowledge, so mixture and quality matter more than model tricks.
A multi-stage data mixture, manually rebalanced between stages in response to monitored benchmarks, beats committing to one fixed mixture for the whole run.
Reserve the highest-quality math and code data for the Warmup-Stable-Decay decay phase and upsample it there — annealing is where specialized data pays off most.
When existing datasets underperform, build better ones: classifier-based educational filtering (an LLM annotates quality, a cheap classifier scales it) produced FineWeb-Edu, FineMath, and Stack-Edu.
Deliberate over-training (~11T tokens into 1.7B, ~2 epochs) trades Chinchilla-optimality for a cheaper-to-serve model — a defensible choice at this scale class.
smollm2-when-smol-goes-big-data-centric-.whyItMatters: SmolLM2 is the closest thing to a blueprint for what Microlab is actually doing: strong small models built on data discipline rather than scale or novel architecture. It ties Phase 1 (curation, tokenization, dedup, decontamination, classifier filtering) directly to Phase 8 (staged mixing, annealing, midtraining) by showing them as one continuous recipe on a model in this lab's exact size class.
smollm2-when-smol-goes-big-data-centric-.phaseConnection: In Phase 1, use it to justify the data-quality pipeline — the reused classifier-filtering pattern, the 60/40 FineWeb-Edu/DCLM web blend, MinHash dedup, and 13-gram decontamination against eval sets. In Phase 8, treat its four-stage rebalancing and WSD decay-phase upsampling as the canonical worked example of annealing/midtraining: how to introduce medium datasets mid-run, reserve the best data for the decay, and let live benchmarks drive each mixture change. Contrast the 1.7B multi-stage recipe with the 135M/360M single-stage recipe to reason about which regime your own models fall in.
suggestedReadingFocus: The four guiding principles in Section 4 as a checklist for any staged pretraining run
The stage-by-stage mixture narrative (Figure 2, Sections 4.2-4.5) and what capability gap each rebalance reacted to
The Warmup-Stable-Decay schedule and why its decay phase is the natural home for annealing
The classifier-based educational filtering pattern reused for FineWeb-Edu, FineMath, and Stack-Edu
The contrast between the 1.7B multi-stage recipe and the 135M/360M single-stage recipe

muon-is-scalable-for-llm-training.oneSentence: Muon replaces AdamW's per-element preconditioning with orthogonalized momentum, and this report shows the two fixes — weight decay plus update-RMS matching — that let it scale to LLMs at roughly 2x AdamW's compute efficiency.
muon-is-scalable-for-llm-training.summary: Muon is the first serious post-AdamW optimizer to be validated at real LLM scale. Instead of AdamW's element-wise adaptive step, Muon treats each weight as a matrix and orthogonalizes its momentum with a cheap Newton-Schulz iteration — flattening the update's singular values so the weight learns in many directions rather than a few dominant ones. Muon already beat AdamW on nanoGPT-speedrun-scale models, but this Moonshot 'Moonlight' report identifies why it stalled when scaled up and fixes it: decoupled weight decay keeps weight and activation RMS inside bf16's precision range, and rescaling each matrix update by 0.2*sqrt(max(A,B)) makes Muon's shape-dependent update RMS match AdamW's ~0.2-0.4 band, so Muon can reuse AdamW's tuned learning rate and weight decay with no extra tuning. Scaling-law experiments on dense 399M-1.5B models fit Muon at 2.506*C^-0.052 vs AdamW at 2.608*C^-0.054, i.e. AdamW-equal loss at ~52% of the FLOPs, and the authors back it up by training a 3B-activated/16B-total MoE on 5.7T tokens that advances the performance-vs-FLOPs Pareto frontier.
coreIdeas: Muon orthogonalizes the momentum matrix via Newton-Schulz (approximating (M M^T)^{-1/2} M = U V^T), keeping its singular vectors but setting singular values to ~1, so updates are diverse across directions instead of concentrated.

Two fixes make Muon scale: decoupled weight decay (keeps weight/activation RMS in bf16 range) and matching Muon's per-parameter update RMS to AdamW's (via 0.2*sqrt(max(A,B)) rescaling, from Lemma 1's RMS = sqrt(1/max(A,B))).

Because the RMS is matched, Muon is a near drop-in for AdamW — it reuses the same learning rate and weight decay, optimizes only 2D weight matrices, and leaves embeddings, the LM head, and norm gains on AdamW.
Scaling laws show ~2x compute efficiency (AdamW-equal loss at ~52% of FLOPs), measured fairly against a grid-searched AdamW baseline rather than a single loss curve.
muon-is-scalable-for-llm-training.whyItMatters: Optimizer choice is one of the few knobs that can shift the whole loss-vs-compute curve, and Muon is the first credible challenger to AdamW that holds up at scale. For a from-scratch lab it is unusually approachable — the core Newton-Schulz orthogonalization is about twenty lines and only touches matrix parameters — so it turns 'is AdamW really optimal?' from a leaderboard claim into an experiment you can run yourself.
muon-is-scalable-for-llm-training.phaseConnection: Read this in Phase 4 (scaling), where your Trainer already uses AdamW. A Muon-vs-AdamW ablation at 10-50M parameters is a natural phase-4 stretch: wire Muon in for the 2D weights (keep AdamW for embeddings, LM head, and norms), reuse your existing AdamW learning rate and weight decay thanks to the update-RMS matching, and compare validation loss at equal FLOPs to see whether the ~2x efficiency story reproduces at your scale. It also connects to your data-sized-model + val-loss validation regime — the honest test of an optimizer is loss at fixed compute, not a single fast run.
suggestedReadingFocus: The Muon update rule and what Newton-Schulz actually computes — the orthogonalization is the entire optimizer.
The two scaling fixes (weight decay; 0.2*sqrt(max(A,B)) update-RMS matching) and why Lemma 1 makes shape-dependent rescaling necessary.
The scaling-law comparison — ~52% of AdamW's FLOPs for equal loss — and how a fair AdamW baseline was built before claiming it.
The matrix-only scope and hybrid Muon+AdamW split, which is exactly how you would wire Muon into an existing AdamW Trainer for an ablation.

scaling-data-constrained-language-models.oneSentence: This paper extends the Chinchilla scaling law to the data-constrained regime, showing across 400+ runs that repeating a fixed corpus for up to ~4 epochs is almost as good as fresh data, that returns decay to near-zero by ~16 epochs (fitted half-life R*_D approximately 15), and that when data is scarce you should train a smaller model for more epochs than Chinchilla prescribes.
scaling-data-constrained-language-models.summary: Chinchilla tells you to scale parameters and tokens in equal proportion, but it assumes every token is unique — one epoch. Muennighoff et al. ask the practitioner's question: what happens when you run out of unique text and have to repeat? They train more than 400 GPT-2-architecture models on C4 subsets (10M-8.7B parameters, up to 900B tokens, up to ~1500 epochs) and fit a modified loss law in which repeated tokens contribute exponentially decaying 'effective data' D' = U_D + U_D*R*_D*(1 - e^(-R_D/R*_D)) and excess parameters contribute a symmetric 'effective parameters' N'. Two learned half-lives govern everything: R*_D approximately 15 for repeated data and R*_N approximately 5 for excess parameters. The consequences are sharp and useful. Repeating for up to ~4 epochs costs almost nothing (the 8.7B/4-epoch model lands within 0.5% of its single-epoch twin); meaningful gains persist to about 16 epochs and then collapse. Because R*_D > R*_N, excess parameters lose value faster than repeated data, so the compute-optimal move under a data budget is to scale epochs faster than parameters — train a smaller model longer (a 27%-smaller-than-Chinchilla model wins at 9.3e21 FLOPs). When repetition is spent, mixing in code (up to ~50%) roughly doubles effective tokens with no natural-language penalty, and perplexity filtering only helps on noisy corpora.
coreIdeas: Repeated tokens are worth exponentially less each pass: D' = U_D + U_D*R*_D*(1 - e^(-R_D/R*_D)) replaces D in the Chinchilla loss, reduces to D at one epoch (R_D=0), and plateaus at U_D*(1 + R*_D) — so no amount of repetition beats having that many unique tokens.

Up to ~4 epochs of repetition is nearly free (negligible loss and downstream difference); returns then diminish and, past the fitted half-life R*_D of about 15 repetitions (~16 epochs), added compute is nearly worthless. At R_D = R*_D a repeated token averages 1 - 1/e (about 0.63) the value of a fresh one.

Excess parameters decay faster than repeated data (R*_N approximately 5 < R*_D approximately 15), so under a data budget you should scale epochs faster than parameters — train a SMALLER model for MORE epochs than Chinchilla suggests; a 27%-smaller-than-optimal model beat the Chinchilla config at 9.3e21 FLOPs on both loss and downstream tasks.

When unique data is exhausted, code augmentation (mixing ~50% Python from The Stack) gives roughly 2x effective tokens with no natural-language degradation, while filtering (perplexity, dedup) only pays off on noisy data — cheaper levers than collecting more unique text.
scaling-data-constrained-language-models.whyItMatters: This is the paper that puts a number on a decision the learner is making right now. The current 150M run trains ~6.4 epochs on TinyStories — about 458M unique tokens repeated toward a ~3B-token budget, i.e. R_D approximately 5.4 repetitions. Plugging that into the paper's own C4-fitted law (R*_D = 15.4) gives an effective-data multiplier of 1 + 15.4*(1 - e^(-5.4/15.4)) approximately 5.55, so those 3B processed tokens are worth roughly 2.5B fresh ones — about an 85% exchange rate, a ~15% repetition tax. That is a comfortable place to be: the run is just past the ~4-epoch 'nearly free' point and still far below the ~16-epoch cliff where returns collapse, so the repetition is a cheap, defensible choice rather than a mistake to fix. Crucially, the paper reframes the instinct to 'just add parameters': because R*_N < R*_D, spending the freed VRAM on a bigger model is a worse use of a fixed corpus than spending it on more epochs (up to the cliff). It is the difference between planning a data budget with a model and guessing.
scaling-data-constrained-language-models.phaseConnection: In Phase 4 (scaling) this law is your data-planning instrument. For the current 150M/TinyStories run it certifies that ~6.4 epochs sits in the benign regime and quantifies the tax (roughly 2.5B effective from 3B processed), so you can decide whether the next increment of compute should buy more epochs, more parameters, or more unique data — the paper's answer being epochs-before-parameters until you near R*_D. For the upcoming ~1B capstone it is decisive: a Chinchilla-optimal 1B model wants ~20B tokens, and if your unique corpus is smaller than that, this law says (1) up to ~4 epochs of repetition is essentially free, (2) you can keep gaining to ~16 epochs but with steep diminishing returns past 4, and (3) you should deliberately pick a somewhat smaller model trained for more epochs over a larger model on the same repeated data. It also hands you two ways to grow the effective budget without new text — code mixing for ~2x effective tokens, and skipping aggressive filtering on clean data — so the capstone's data plan can be sized rather than guessed.
suggestedReadingFocus: Section 3.1 and Appendix A: the effective-data equation D' = U_D + U_D*R*_D*(1 - e^(-R_D/R*_D)) and its derivation as a geometric series of exponentially decaying repetition values — this single formula is the tool you apply to your own epoch counts.

Section 6 and Figure 5: the '~4 epochs nearly free, ~16 epochs cliff' return curves, and the R*_D approximately 15 half-life — the numbers you use to judge the 150M run's 6.4 epochs and to size the capstone's epoch budget.
Section 5 and Figure 3: the IsoLoss contours showing epochs should be scaled faster than parameters (R*_N < R*_D), the direct answer to 'should I spend freed VRAM on a bigger model or more epochs?'
Section 7 and Figure 6: code augmentation for ~2x effective tokens and when filtering helps — the complementary levers for the capstone when pure repetition is exhausted.

Appendix B, Equation 17/20: the fitted C4 constants (A=521, B=1488, E=1.87, alpha=beta=0.353, R*_D=15.4, R*_N=5.3, U_N=0.051*U_D) if you want to actually compute predicted loss for a candidate (U_D, R_D, N) plan.

yarn-efficient-context-window-extension-.oneSentence: YaRN extends the context window of RoPE models by interpolating only the low-frequency rotary dimensions and leaving the high-frequency ones alone, plus a cheap attention-temperature term — the production refinement of plain position interpolation.
yarn-efficient-context-window-extension-.summary: YaRN is what plain Position Interpolation becomes once you stop treating every RoPE frequency the same. Plain PI compresses all rotary positions by a single scale factor s = L'/L, which is exactly the interpolated_rope_cache you hand-write in Phase 8 — simple, but it crushes the high-frequency dimensions the model needs for local token order and stalls around s=8. YaRN keeps the interpolation idea but routes it through each dimension's wavelength: dimensions whose wavelength exceeds the pretrained context (they only ever encode absolute position) get interpolated, while short-wavelength dimensions that encode local relative distance are left untouched, blended by a smooth ramp (NTK-by-parts). It then multiplies the attention logits by a temperature — applied for free by length-scaling q and k — to counteract the entropy that interpolation adds. The result reaches 128k context with ~10x fewer tokens and ~2.5x fewer steps than PI, extrapolates beyond its own fine-tuning length, and stays a pure embedding trick compatible with Flash Attention 2.
coreIdeas: Uniformly scaling every RoPE frequency by s (plain PI) destroys high-frequency information and caps context extension around s=8; the fix is to treat frequencies unequally.

The wavelength lambda_d = 2*pi/theta_d and ratio r(d) = L/lambda_d separate rotary dimensions into absolute-position (long wavelength, interpolate) and local-order (short wavelength, leave alone) — NTK-by-parts interpolates via a ramp gamma over r.
A single attention-softmax temperature (sqrt(1/t) = 0.1*ln(s)+1 for Llama), implemented as a length-scaling of q and k, counteracts interpolation's entropy increase at zero runtime cost.

Because YaRN only modifies precomputed RoPE tables and the query/key scale, it adds no overhead, is a drop-in replacement for PI, and stays Flash-Attention-2 compatible — with Dynamic Scaling it extends context >2x without any fine-tuning.
yarn-efficient-context-window-extension-.whyItMatters: YaRN is the bridge from the toy position-interpolation exercise to the real thing shipped in production long-context models. It shows that the leap from 'scale all frequencies by s' to a genuinely good long-context method is small in code but conceptually precise: reason about RoPE per-dimension by wavelength, and correct the attention distribution the interpolation distorts.
yarn-efficient-context-window-extension-.phaseConnection: Read in Phase 8 (continued pretraining / long context) right after you hand-write plain position interpolation (interpolated_rope_cache with positions and scale). Frame YaRN as what that code becomes when RoPE frequencies are treated unequally: NTK-by-parts (interpolate low-frequency dims, leave high-frequency dims) plus attention-temperature scaling — the scheme Qwen and DeepSeek use for their long-context variants.
suggestedReadingFocus: How plain PI (g(m)=s*m, h(theta)=theta) maps onto your interpolated_rope_cache, and what specifically breaks as s grows
The wavelength/ratio argument for which dimensions to interpolate versus preserve, and the NTK-by-parts ramp gamma(r) with cutoffs alpha, beta
The attention temperature: the softmax(.../ (t*sqrt(|D|))) form, the sqrt(1/t) length-scaling implementation, and the entropy justification
Dynamic Scaling for inference-time extension and the KV-cache caveat (cache pre-RoPE embeddings)

better-faster-large-language-models-via-.oneSentence: Multi-token prediction adds n independent heads on a shared trunk to predict tokens t+1..t+n at once, an overhead-free auxiliary objective that improves sample efficiency at scale and turns the extra heads into a built-in self-speculative draft.
better-faster-large-language-models-via-.summary: In Phase 2 you hand-wrote the next-token cross-entropy loss and trained a tiny GPT with it. This paper is the first thing in the curriculum that changes that objective itself rather than the architecture, data, or optimizer. Gloeckle et al. keep a single shared transformer trunk but attach n small output heads and one shared unembedding, so at every position the model predicts the next n tokens in parallel; assuming the heads are conditionally independent given the trunk's latent, the loss is just a sum of n per-head cross-entropies, and head 1 is exactly the next-token head you already have. A careful sequential forward/backward over the heads keeps peak memory at O(V + d) instead of O(nV + d), so the auxiliary objective is essentially free at matched parameters. The payoff is scale-dependent and honest about it: multi-token prediction hurts small models and only pays off as they grow, with the largest gains on generative and coding benchmarks (13B models solve ~12% more HumanEval and ~17% more MBPP problems) and on byte-level, induction, and algorithmic-reasoning tasks. The same heads that sharpen pretraining double as a draft for self-speculative decoding, giving up to 3x faster inference with no separate draft model — the reason this paper is your bridge from the loss function to Phase 6.
coreIdeas: Generalize L1 = -sum log P(x_{t+1}|context) to L_n predicting the next n tokens; conditional independence given the shared latent factorizes it into a sum of n per-head cross-entropies.
One shared trunk plus one shared unembedding plus n cheap heads (head 1 = the ordinary next-token head) means the change is small to bolt onto an existing GPT.

A sequential per-head forward/backward that accumulates gradients into the trunk before freeing each head's logits keeps memory at O(V + d), so the auxiliary loss adds no training-time or memory overhead.
Benefits grow with model size and concentrate on generative, coding, and reasoning tasks — it can even slightly hurt small models and multiple-choice/likelihood benchmarks.
The auxiliary heads become a self-speculative draft at inference (blockwise parallel / Medusa-style), delivering up to 3x speedups without a separate draft model.

Intuition for why it helps: it up-weights high-information 'choice point' tokens (weight n(n+1)/2) and doubles the effective weight on mutual information, narrowing the teacher-forcing vs. autoregressive distribution gap.
better-faster-large-language-models-via-.whyItMatters: It is the first objective-level departure from the next-token loss you just implemented — a concrete, low-cost way to see that the training objective is itself a design choice, not a fixed given. It also grounds the idea that a single mechanism (extra prediction heads) can serve both better pretraining and faster inference, which is why DeepSeek-V3 shipped a single-extra-head (MTP-1) variant in production pretraining.
better-faster-large-language-models-via-.phaseConnection: Read it in Phase 2 (tiny GPT pretraining) right after implementing standard next-token cross-entropy: it shows how to extend that exact loss with auxiliary heads, while being candid that a tiny model may not benefit. It is also the direct bridge to Phase 6, where the same heads reappear as the draft model for speculative decoding.
suggestedReadingFocus: The loss generalization from L1 to L_n and the conditional-independence factorization into n per-head cross-entropies (Section 2).
The memory-efficient sequential head forward/backward that makes the objective overhead-free, and why it depends on V >> d.
The scale dependence of the gains and the honest caveat that small models can be hurt (Sections 3.1, 3.7).
How the auxiliary heads enable self-speculative decoding, connecting this objective to Phase 6 inference speedups (Sections 2 inference, 3.2).

native-sparse-attention-hardware-aligned.oneSentence: NSA is DeepSeek's natively-trainable sparse attention — three learned branches (compressed coarse tokens, top-n selected fine blocks, a sliding window) mixed by a gate — that shrinks attention COMPUTE at long context and is optimized end-to-end during pretraining rather than bolted on at inference.
native-sparse-attention-hardware-aligned.summary: Phase 6 asks a sharp follow-up to the KV-cache work: once GQA and MQA have shrunk the memory footprint of the cache, what shrinks the attention COMPUTE that still grows with sequence length? NSA is the answer. Instead of attending over every past token, each query is routed through three parallel branches — token compression (coarse block-level summaries built by a learnable MLP), blockwise token selection (keep only the top-n most important fine-grained blocks, ranked for free from the compression scores), and a sliding window (recent local context in its own branch) — whose outputs a learned per-branch gate combines. The critical word is NATIVELY: the whole path is differentiable and trained from scratch, because post-hoc pruning pushes a model off its pretrained trajectory (top-20% attention covers only ~70% of the scores) and non-differentiable selectors like k-means or SimHash break gradient flow. The second half of the paper is pure inference engineering: a GQA-aware Triton kernel that loads all heads of a group together, fetches their shared sparse KV blocks contiguously, and schedules on Triton's grid, so theoretical sparsity becomes real wall-clock speedup (up to 11.6x decode, 9.0x forward, 6.0x backward at 64k) while a 27B model matches or beats Full Attention on quality. DeepSeek productionized this direction in DeepSeek V4 (April 2026), whose hybrid compressed sparse attention holds roughly 10% of the KV cache at 1M-token context — NSA is the research paper that lineage traces back to.
coreIdeas: Attention has two costs and they need separate fixes: GQA/MQA cut the KV-cache MEMORY, but attention COMPUTE (and per-token KV loads at decode) still scale with length — that is the gap NSA closes.

Three branches under one gate: compression gives cheap global context (and the scores that drive selection), selection recovers fine-grained detail via top-n whole blocks, and a dedicated sliding-window branch handles local context without shortcutting the others.

Sparsity must be trained in, not bolted on: differentiable, natively-learned selection avoids the accuracy loss and broken gradients of post-hoc pruning, and lets NSA actually beat Full Attention on reasoning and long-context tasks.

Hardware-aligned or it doesn't count: blockwise (not per-token) selection plus a group-centric Triton kernel that shares KV loads across a GQA group is what turns theoretical FLOP savings into 6-11.6x real speedups.
native-sparse-attention-hardware-aligned.whyItMatters: NSA is Phase 6's cleanest bridge from 'store the KV cache more cheaply' (GQA/MQA, paging) to 'compute attention more cheaply at long context.' It shows that sparse attention only pays off when the algorithm is co-designed with the kernel and the training pipeline — the recurring inference-engineering lesson that a theoretical win means nothing until it survives contact with Tensor Cores, shared KV groups, and gradient flow. Its production sequel, DeepSeek V4 (April 2026), keeps only ~10% of the KV cache at 1M context using hybrid compressed sparse attention, making NSA the reference point for where long-context inference is actually heading.
native-sparse-attention-hardware-aligned.phaseConnection: Read it after the GQA/MQA and KV-cache material in Phase 6: NSA is the compute-side complement to those memory-side wins. Use it to reason about the full long-context inference stack — how compression, selection, and windowing trade off against each other, why blockwise access and group-shared KV selection are non-negotiable on GPUs, and how a natively-trained sparse model scales to the 1M-context, ~10%-cache regime that DeepSeek V4 productionized.
suggestedReadingFocus: The compute-bound (training/prefill) vs memory-bound (decode) split from Section 3.1 — it explains why NSA targets FLOPs in one phase and KV loads in the other
The three-branch framework and gate (Eq. 5), and why the sliding window needs its own independent keys and values
How compression attention scores are reused to rank selection blocks for free, and why importance is summed across a GQA group so all heads pick the same blocks
The kernel design (group-centric loading, shared KV fetching, grid scheduling) as the concrete mechanism that makes sparsity fast on real hardware
The efficiency numbers (11.6x decode / 9.0x forward / 6.0x backward at 64k) and how they set up the DeepSeek V4 ~10%-cache-at-1M-context production result

efficient-streaming-language-models-with.oneSentence: Autoregressive LLMs dump a large, meaningless share of their attention onto the first few tokens — "attention sinks" forced by softmax summing to one — so evicting those tokens (as naive sliding-window caches do) collapses the model; StreamingLLM fixes it by pinning ~4 initial sink tokens alongside a rolling recent window, streaming stably over 4M+ tokens at up to 22.2x the speed of recomputation, no fine-tuning.
efficient-streaming-language-models-with.summary: Xiao et al. start from exactly the failure the learner is about to hit: a fixed-capacity KV cache that must evict tokens to keep streaming. The obvious eviction policy — window attention, keep only the most recent L tokens' KV — collapses the instant the very first tokens fall out, with Llama-2-13B perplexity jumping from 5.40 to over 5000 at the eviction boundary, not degrading smoothly. Visualizing attention maps reveals why: beyond the bottom couple of layers, nearly every head pours attention onto the initial tokens regardless of their content. The authors name these "attention sinks" and trace them to softmax, whose denominator forces attention weights to sum to one — so a query with no strong match must offload its surplus attention somewhere, and the initial tokens, visible to every later position under the causal mask, get trained into that role. The fix is small: keep the KV of a handful of initial sink tokens (four is the ablated sweet spot; one or two is not enough, more barely helps) permanently pinned, and slide a rolling window over the rest. This restores near-oracle perplexity across Llama-2, MPT, Falcon, and Pythia over 4 million+ tokens at O(TL) cost and up to 22.2x the speed of sliding-window-with-recomputation. A clean control — swapping the first tokens for linebreak "\n" tokens still works — shows sinks are an absolute-position artifact, not about meaning. Pretraining with a single dedicated learnable sink token collapses the requirement to that one token with no downstream cost, the direction production models (e.g., GPT-OSS attention sinks) later took. The crucial caveat: StreamingLLM does not extend context or add memory — it streams coherently over what is still cached and cannot recall evicted content.
coreIdeas: Softmax attention must sum to one over all context, so a query with no strong match still has to dump its surplus attention somewhere — and under causal masking the initial tokens, visible to every later position, become that sink.

Naive window attention collapses not gradually but exactly when the first tokens are evicted, because removing the sinks tears a large piece out of the softmax denominator and shifts the attention distribution far from what the model saw in training.

Pinning ~4 initial sink tokens plus a rolling recent window restores near-oracle perplexity with no fine-tuning; ablations show one or two sinks are insufficient, four is the threshold, and more give diminishing returns.
Sinks are about absolute position, not content: replacing the first tokens with linebreak "\n" tokens still restores streaming, so any four leading slots can serve as sinks.

Positions in the rolling cache are assigned by slot within the cache, not by original text index (for RoPE, cache Keys pre-rotation and rotate per-step by cache position) — this is what lets a finite-window model stream past its pretraining length, though it does not add real long-context memory.
efficient-streaming-language-models-with.whyItMatters: This is the paper that explains what the learner's just-built fixed-capacity KV cache teaches the moment they try to evict from it. The intuitive fix — slide the window, drop the oldest tokens at block_size — silently guts the softmax denominator and makes the model output garbage, and StreamingLLM names the reason (attention sinks) and the four-line remedy (pin the first few slots, roll the rest). It converts a mysterious 'why does my streaming model fall apart' bug into a precise, implementable cache-eviction policy, and it is the mechanism behind the attention-sink slots now baked into production models like GPT-OSS. It also draws a hard line the learner must respect: this stabilizes generation over the cache, it does not lengthen context.
efficient-streaming-language-models-with.phaseConnection: Phase 6 (inference engineering), read right after hand-writing the fixed-capacity KV cache that simply stops at block_size. Use it to turn eviction from a model-breaking hack into a correct policy: split the cache into pinned sink slots and a rolling window, get the within-cache positional encoding right (the RoPE recompute is the part that bites), and confirm with a perplexity-over-length curve that the collapse at the eviction boundary is gone. It pairs naturally with the PagedAttention reading — one gives the eviction policy, the other the block-level memory structure — and sets up the boundary between streaming stability and true context-window extension.
suggestedReadingFocus: Section 3.1 and Figure 3: read the softmax-sums-to-one argument until you can explain why the surplus attention lands on the initial tokens specifically, and why window attention's perplexity jumps ~1000x exactly at the eviction boundary rather than drifting.

Section 3.2: the cache layout (four pinned sinks + rolling window) and, most importantly, the positional-encoding rule — positions assigned by cache slot, not original text index, with RoPE Keys cached before rotation. This is the part reimplementations get wrong.
Table 2 ablation: why four sink tokens and not one, and why more than four barely helps — this is the number you will hardcode into the eviction policy.

Section 3.3 and the conclusion: the single learnable sink token (and its link to SoftMax-off-by-One) as the pretraining-time version production models adopted, and the explicit scope limit that StreamingLLM stabilizes generation over the cache but does not extend context or recall evicted tokens.

eagle-speculative-sampling-requires-reth.oneSentence: EAGLE turns speculative decoding into a production-grade lever by drafting at the second-to-top-layer FEATURE level with a single lightweight head bolted onto the target model's own hidden states — conditioned on the token sampled one step ahead to resolve feature uncertainty, and verified as a tree in one target pass — for a lossless 2.7x-3.5x speedup with no fine-tuning of the target.
eagle-speculative-sampling-requires-reth.summary: In Phase 6 you hand-write the Leviathan accept/reject rule and prove it samples from the target distribution unchanged. EAGLE is what that idea becomes in production, and it changes only the DRAFT stage while inheriting that exact verification rule. Its two observations reframe drafting. First, autoregression is easier at the FEATURE level — the second-to-top-layer hidden state, just before the LM head — than at the token level, because feature sequences are more regular than the token strings they decode into. Second, feature-level autoregression is under-determined: since the target samples its next token, the same feature can be followed by different next features depending on which token was drawn, so a draft that sees only past features cannot pick the branch. EAGLE fixes this by feeding the draft the token sequence advanced by one step — the already-sampled token that disambiguates the branch. The draft model is tiny and needs no separate network: it reuses the frozen target embedding and LM head and adds only an Autoregression Head (one FC layer that fuses the concatenated feature+token vector back to hidden size, plus one transformer decoder layer). It emits a tree-structured draft with tree attention, and the target verifies the whole tree in a single forward pass with a SpecInfer-style recursive speculative-sampling rule that provably preserves the output distribution for greedy and non-greedy alike. The payoff: 1.7x-2.1x over Lookahead, 1.5x-1.6x over Medusa, and 2.7x-3.5x over vanilla on LLaMA2-Chat 70B, all without touching the target's weights.
coreIdeas: Draft at the FEATURE level, not with a separate model: autoregress the target's own second-to-top-layer hidden states with a lightweight head, then reuse the frozen LM head to decode tokens — feature sequences are more regular than token strings, so a small head extrapolates them accurately (~0.8 vs Medusa's ~0.6).

Resolve feature uncertainty by conditioning on the shifted token: sampling makes the next feature ambiguous given only past features, so EAGLE feeds in the token advanced by one time step (the sampled outcome); this single change is the largest ablation gain, lifting speedup from ~1.9x to ~2.8x.

The head is minimal overhead: reuse the target's frozen embedding and LM head, concatenate feature+token to 2*hidden_dim, one FC layer back to hidden_dim, one decoder layer out (0.24B-0.99B params, trained on 2-4B tokens with Smooth-L1 feature regression + 0.1-weighted classification loss and U(-0.1,0.1) feature-noise augmentation).

Tree drafts verified in one pass keep the speedup lossless: EAGLE drafts a depth-m tree with more than m tokens via tree attention and the target validates the whole tree in one forward pass, applying the recursive accept/reject rule at each node so the output distribution provably equals the target's for greedy AND non-greedy decoding — no target fine-tuning.
eagle-speculative-sampling-requires-reth.whyItMatters: The owner flagged this paper specifically: speculative decoding is increasingly the production performance lever, and EAGLE is its default modern form. Phase 6 teaches WHY speculation is lossless (the accept/reject rule and its proof); EAGLE teaches the part that actually moved the needle in real serving — a draft good enough to matter, built for free out of the target model's own features. It embodies the lab's no-fallbacks stance: it does not approximate or fine-tune the target and quietly drift the distribution; it stays provably exact and buys latency honestly. It also makes concrete why draft quality is the whole game — acceptance rate alpha times zero overhead is the only thing that turns into wall-clock speedup — and it composes cleanly with quantization/compilation (EAGLE + gpt-fast reaches 160.4 tokens/s on an RTX 3090). This is the paper that made speculative decoding a default rather than a research curiosity.
eagle-speculative-sampling-requires-reth.phaseConnection: This sits directly downstream of the Phase 6 speculative-decoding exercise: you already implemented Leviathan's accept/reject rule and proved its losslessness, and EAGLE keeps that verification stage verbatim while upgrading only the draft. Read it to understand the arc the field actually took: EAGLE-1 (this paper) — feature-level autoregression + shifted-token conditioning + a static draft tree; EAGLE-2 — context-aware DYNAMIC draft trees that shape and prune branches by the draft's own confidence scores; EAGLE-3 — dropping the feature-regression constraint via a training-time test and fusing low/middle/high multi-layer features for direct token prediction, which unlocks data scaling and pushes acceptance lengths (and speedups) higher. That 1->2->3 progression is why the EAGLE family is the default speculative path in vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM. It also connects back to Phase 14 (distillation): both build a draft/student that mirrors a teacher's distribution — but EAGLE mines the mirror out of the target's own hidden states instead of training a standalone model.
suggestedReadingFocus: Confirm the verification stage is the Phase 6 rule you already wrote: Section 2 (Preliminaries) and 3.3 — EAGLE inherits the exact accept/reject / recursive speculative-sampling rule, so its speedup is lossless by construction; only the draft changed.

The two observations that reframe drafting: feature-level > token-level (Observation 1, Figure 4) and feature uncertainty resolved by the one-step-advanced token (Observation 2, Figure 3) — the conceptual core of the paper.

The Autoregression Head data path in Section 3.1 / Figure 6: frozen embedding + LM head reused, feature+token concatenated to 2*hidden_dim, FC down, one decoder layer — and why this minimal overhead is what lets acceptance rate translate into real latency wins.
Tree attention as the production replacement for a linear draft chain (Sections 3.1, 3.3), and the ablations in 4.3 showing the shifted token and tree verification are where the speedup comes from.

Read this as EAGLE-1 and hold the family arc in mind: EAGLE-2 (dynamic, context-aware draft trees) and EAGLE-3 (training-time test + multi-layer feature fusion, direct token prediction) — the path that made EAGLE the default speculative decoder in vLLM/SGLang/TensorRT-LLM.

sparse-autoencoders-find-highly-interpre.oneSentence: Cunningham et al. resolve superposition by training a sparse autoencoder on a model's residual-stream activations, learning an overcomplete dictionary whose features are more monosemantic and interpretable than neurons, and causally localise the IOI circuit better than PCA.
sparse-autoencoders-find-highly-interpre.summary: This is the natural next rung above the logit-lens and induction-head analysis you do in this phase. Those tools read the residual stream in the model's own neuron basis; this paper argues that basis is the wrong one. Neurons are polysemantic — they fire for several unrelated things — because of superposition: a d-dimensional layer stores far more than d features by packing them into an overcomplete set of near-orthogonal directions rather than onto individual neurons, which only works when features fire sparsely. Recovering those directions is sparse dictionary learning, and the whole method is a one-hidden-layer autoencoder over cached activations x: encode c = ReLU(Mx + b), decode x_hat = M^T c (tied, row-normalised weights so features stay unit-norm), and minimise ||x - x_hat||_2^2 + alpha ||c||_1. The overcompleteness ratio R = d_hid / d_in lets the dictionary hold more features than the layer has dimensions; the L1 coefficient alpha — not the reconstruction term — is what pressures the codes to be sparse and recover the generating features. They validate the dictionary three ways: interpretability (GPT-4 autointerpretation scores beat neurons, PCA, and ICA at every layer, fading with depth), causality (patching ACDC-selected dictionary directions on the Indirect Object Identification task reaches a target KL with fewer patches and smaller edits than PCA, while a non-sparse alpha=0 dictionary does not), and case studies of individual monosemantic features — an apostrophe feature whose ablation specifically suppresses the 's' logit, and a closing-parenthesis feature with a clean cross-layer circuit. It is honest about the cost: reconstruction is lossy (substituting a reconstructed layer raises Pile perplexity from 25 to 40), and the pipeline is residual-stream-first, not yet robust inside MLPs.
coreIdeas: Superposition explains polysemantic neurons: a layer represents more features than it has dimensions by assigning them to an overcomplete set of directions, feasible only when features are sparse — so recovering features is sparse dictionary learning, not reading the neuron basis.

The method is a single-hidden-layer autoencoder on cached activations: c = ReLU(Mx + b), x_hat = M^T c = sum_i c_i f_i, trained with L(x) = ||x - x_hat||_2^2 + alpha ||c||_1, with tied encoder/decoder weights and row-normalised dictionary features.

Two knobs govern everything: the ratio R = d_hid / d_in sets overcompleteness (R > 1 holds more features than dimensions), and alpha weights the L1 sparsity term that, not the MSE, is what drives monosemanticity and feature recovery — and row-normalising M stops the model cheating the L1 penalty by rescaling features.

Interpretability is measured automatically (Bills et al.): a model describes a feature from its top activations then predicts its activation on new text, and the correlation is the score — dictionary features beat neurons, random directions, PCA, and ICA at every layer, most in early layers.

Causality is shown by activation patching on IOI: patch ACDC-ordered dictionary directions via x'_i = x_i + sum (c-bar - c) f_j and reach a target KL with fewer patches and smaller edits than PCA; the alpha=0 control proves sparsity, not the autoencoder alone, is responsible.

Honest limits: reconstruction is imperfect (Pile perplexity 25 to 40 when a layer is replaced by its reconstruction), the method works on the residual stream but not yet robustly inside MLPs, and the long-term motivation is enumerative safety — a complete feature list that could certify against deception.
sparse-autoencoders-find-highly-interpre.whyItMatters: Your logit lens and induction-head work read the residual stream in the model's own coordinates; this paper is the argument that those coordinates are a bad basis, and gives you an unsupervised, cheap way to find a better one. It also raises your interpretability bar the same way the tuned lens and ROME did: a feature claim is only worth making if you validate it three ways — what activates the feature (input), what ablating it does to the logits (output), and what upstream features cause it (circuit). That input/output/circuit discipline, plus the finding that a sparse overcomplete dictionary is more monosemantic than any neuron, is a lens you can point straight at the 150M you trained from scratch.
sparse-autoencoders-find-highly-interpre.phaseConnection: Phase 5 (interpretability): read this right after your hand-written logit lens and induction-head scorers are running on your 150M. The stretch project is unusually tractable because you already collect the raw material — collect_residual_stream returns the post-embedding and post-block residual states, so cache a few million of those vectors from a validation slice as your training set x. Then train a tiny sparse autoencoder over them: c = ReLU(Mx + b), x_hat = M^T c, loss ||x - x_hat||_2^2 + alpha ||c||_1, with tied weights, row-normalised M, an overcompleteness ratio R of maybe 4-8x your d_model, and a small alpha you tune by watching sparsity versus reconstruction. Validate exactly as the paper does but by hand: pick a few high-activation features, read the text that fires them (input), ablate one from the residual stream and read the logit change through your existing lens (output), and — if you have time — trace which earlier-layer features drive it (circuit). Expect the paper's caveats to bite: reconstruction will be lossy, so measure the perplexity hit from substituting the reconstruction, and stick to the residual stream rather than MLP internals for your first attempt.
suggestedReadingFocus: The four-equation core (Eq 1-4) and each term — the ReLU encoder, the tied M^T decoder, row-normalisation, and why the L1 penalty (not the reconstruction loss) is what recovers features.

The two hyperparameters you will actually set on your own model: the overcompleteness ratio R = d_hid / d_in and the sparsity coefficient alpha, and how they trade reconstruction against monosemanticity.

The autointerpretation metric and the Figure 2 baseline comparison (dictionary features vs neurons, PCA, ICA), since it is the headline evidence and defines what 'more interpretable' means quantitatively.

The IOI activation-patching experiment (Section 4) — the patch formula, ACDC feature ordering, and the alpha=0 control — as the template for causally validating features rather than just eyeballing activations.

The Section 5 input/output/circuit case studies and the Section 6 limitations (lossy reconstruction, residual-stream-only) so your expectations for a home-grown SAE on your 150M are calibrated before you start.

swe-bench-can-language-models-resolve-re.oneSentence: SWE-bench asks whether language models can resolve 2,294 real GitHub issues from 12 popular Python repositories by generating a patch for the full codebase that is graded by re-running the repository's own tests — a benchmark whose best model at publication resolved only 1.96% of issues, making it the execution-verified yardstick that agentic coding is measured against.
swe-bench-can-language-models-resolve-re.summary: SWE-bench reframes code evaluation from 'can the model write a self-contained function' to 'can the model resolve a real issue inside a real repository.' Each task instance hands the model an actual GitHub issue plus a snapshot of the whole codebase at the pre-fix commit; the model must emit a patch that, once applied with unix `patch`, makes the repository's test suite pass. The construction is a three-stage funnel: scrape ~90,000 pull requests from 12 well-maintained Python projects, keep only merged PRs that both close an issue and modify test files, then keep only those where at least one test flips from fail to pass and the project installs and runs cleanly — 90,000 PRs collapse to 2,294 instances. Grading is entirely execution-based and is the heart of the design: an instance is resolved only if the patch applies AND every fail-to-pass test (which the fix is supposed to make pass) plus a median of 51 pass-to-pass tests (which guard existing behavior) all succeed. That contract is exactly a phase-0 eval harness — deterministic, test-driven, no partial credit for plausible-looking output — scaled from a single prompt up to a codebase of thousands of files and 438K lines. The difficulty is brutal precisely because the signal is tiny: gold patches average 32.8 edited lines across 1.7 files and 3.0 functions, buried in enormous context that no window holds, so files must be retrieved (BM25, since dense retrieval fails on long code queried with natural language) and then localized. At publication Claude 2 resolved 1.96% under BM25 (Claude 3 Opus later reaches 3.79%), and performance falls as context grows because models cannot find the lines to touch. The authors deliberately leave agent-based and tool-augmented methods as future work — which is exactly where this lab is headed.
coreIdeas: A task instance = (issue text + full codebase snapshot) in, a patch file out; the patch is applied and the repository's real unit/system tests are executed to decide pass or fail. There is no textual comparison to the gold patch — any fix that makes the tests pass counts, and any fix that does not, fails.

Grading uses two test sets: fail-to-pass tests (failed before the gold fix, must pass after — proving the issue is resolved; every instance has >=1, 40% have >=2) and pass-to-pass tests (a median of 51 that must stay green — proving nothing else broke). This is execution-verified evaluation with a strict, no-partial-credit contract.

The three-stage construction pipeline (scrape ~90,000 PRs, attribute-filter to merged issue-resolving PRs that touch test files, execution-filter to instances with a genuine fail-to-pass flip that installs cleanly) is what makes the benchmark self-verifying and continually refreshable to dodge training-data contamination.

Difficulty comes from scale and localization, not from writing clever code: codebases average 3,010 non-test files and 438K lines while gold patches average only 32.8 lines across 1.7 files, so relevant files must be retrieved (BM25 vs an unrealistic 'oracle' of the actually-edited files) and the handful of buggy lines localized — and model performance drops as context length grows.

The headline is deliberately near-zero (Claude 2 at 1.96% under BM25, 4.8% with oracle retrieval; Claude 3 Opus 3.79%): a non-saturated benchmark with enormous headroom, whose authors explicitly point to agent-based and tool-augmented approaches as the way to climb it.
swe-bench-can-language-models-resolve-re.whyItMatters: SWE-bench is the destination benchmark for this lab's turn toward code and agents. Every earlier phase — the story-based pretraining, the evals, the inference work — builds a model that eventually has to do something economically real, and 'resolve a GitHub issue that the repo's own tests certify' is the cleanest, hardest, most honest definition of that available. Just as importantly, SWE-bench is a design lesson: it is the phase-0 harness philosophy taken to its logical extreme. Phase 0 teaches that a good eval runs the artifact and checks an objective outcome rather than trusting a similarity score or an LLM judge (the exact 'fallbacks mask bugs' failure mode this lab avoids). SWE-bench proves that same principle survives contact with the messiest possible task: 2,294 real repositories, real dependencies, real test suites, and a binary resolved/not-resolved verdict with no room to fake it. It also exposes the specific failure the whole agentic-coding field is organized around — models cannot localize the few lines to edit inside a huge context — which is the problem retrieval, scaffolding, and tool use in Phase 15 exist to attack. Understanding why the naive baselines score ~2% is understanding why agents are necessary at all.
swe-bench-can-language-models-resolve-re.phaseConnection: Read in Phase 15 (tool use and agentic behavior), where the lab moves from generating text to acting on a repository. The direct connection is that Phase 15 is where you stop asking a model for a patch in one shot (the near-0% baseline this paper reports) and start giving it tools — read files, run tests, search the codebase, iterate — to close the localization gap SWE-bench exposes. The backward connection is to Phase 0: SWE-bench's apply-patch-then-run-the-tests grader is the same execution-verified harness you first built for functional-correctness evals (the HumanEval lineage), so treat SWE-bench as that harness scaled from one function to a whole repo, with fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass sets replacing a single assertion. Practically, when you build or run an agentic coding loop in this lab, SWE-bench (or the 300-instance SWE-bench Lite subset, curated for more self-contained bug fixes) is the yardstick you report against — and the paper's construction pipeline is the template for minting your own execution-verified tasks so your evaluation set can outrun contamination.
suggestedReadingFocus: Section 2.1 and Figure 2 — the three-stage construction pipeline. Internalize why a valid instance must be a merged, issue-resolving PR that also modifies test files and yields a fail-to-pass flip; this is the recipe for building your own self-verifying tasks.

Section 2.2 — the exact grading contract (apply patch, run fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests, resolved only if all pass). Map this onto the Phase 0 eval harness you already built and note what changes when the unit under test is a repository instead of a function.

Table 1 and Section 2.3 — the scale statistics (195-word issues, 3,010 files, 438K lines, versus 32.8-line gold patches). This quantifies the localization-in-noise problem that motivates retrieval and, later, agents.

Section 4.1 and Section 5 — BM25 vs 'oracle' retrieval and the finding that resolution rate drops as context length grows. This is the empirical case that one-shot generation is insufficient and that the Phase 15 tooling is required, not optional.

Section 7 (Discussion/Limitations) — the authors explicitly defer agent-based and tool-augmented methods and warn that execution-based testing alone does not guarantee good code. Read this as the mandate for what Phase 15 attempts and a caution about the limits of any test-only grader.

tau-bench-a-benchmark-for-tool-agent-use.oneSentence: tau-bench evaluates agents that must converse with a simulated user and call domain APIs under written policy constraints, and introduces pass^k to measure whether an agent succeeds reliably across k independent trials rather than just once.
tau-bench-a-benchmark-for-tool-agent-use.summary: tau-bench makes agentic evaluation realistic by forcing an agent to do three things at once: interrogate an LM-simulated user for intents and details, act on databases only through domain API tools, and obey a written policy document of rules it must enforce itself. Each episode is graded objectively by comparing the final database state to a unique annotated goal state, so an open-ended conversation stays verifiable. Its lasting contribution to Microlab is pass^k: the probability that all k i.i.d. trials of a task succeed. Where pass@1 rewards a single lucky rollout, pass^k exposes that even the best function-calling agents are unreliable — gpt-4o solves under 50% of tasks at pass^1 and falls below 25% at pass^8 in retail.
coreIdeas: Realistic agent tasks require gathering information from a user over many turns, not receiving one complete instruction up front — so the benchmark pairs each agent with an LM-simulated user that has a hidden intent.
Rule-following is a first-class capability: the agent is given a domain policy it must self-enforce, and evaluation checks the resulting database state, not the agent's stated reasoning.

pass^k measures reliability (all k trials succeed) rather than discovery (pass@k, at least one of k succeeds); consistency across independent rollouts is the property that matters for a user-facing agent.
A strong pass^1 can completely mask fragility: gpt-4o looks acceptable on one trial but collapses below 25% pass^8 on retail, so a single passing rollout is not evidence an agent works.
tau-bench-a-benchmark-for-tool-agent-use.whyItMatters: tau-bench is the reference for how to think about evaluating agents that take real actions under rules. It reframes success from 'did one rollout work' to 'does it work every time', and gives a concrete, unbiased estimator (pass^k) for that question — the exact mindset Phase 15 needs once its agents can call tools at all.
tau-bench-a-benchmark-for-tool-agent-use.phaseConnection: Your Phase 15 exercises score schema-validity and single-run task success — the pass@1 view. tau-bench is the lesson that this is not enough: run each agentic task k times and report pass^k, so an agent that passes one lucky rollout but violates policy or hallucinates arguments on the next is caught. Use it to justify multi-trial harnesses, an objective end-state check for tool tasks, and a policy/rule-following dimension alongside raw task success.
